title: NEC Articles 100–110 — Definitions & General Requirements
description: Key definitions from Article 100 and general installation requirements from Article 110. 30 questions.

questions.question: What is the definition of 'Ampacity'?
choices: The maximum current a conductor can carry continuously without exceeding its insulation voltage rating
The current in amperes that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating
The short-circuit current rating of a conductor based on its cross-sectional area
The rated load current of the overcurrent protective device protecting the conductor
questions.answer: The current in amperes that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Ampacity as the maximum current, in amperes, that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating. Conditions of use include ambient temperature, number of conductors in a raceway, and installation method, all of which affect the ampacity.

questions.question: Equipment or materials described as 'Approved' means which of the following?
choices: Listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (NRTL)
Labeled with a mark from a product certification organization
Acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ)
Compliant with the applicable product standard published by ANSI
questions.answer: Acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ)
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines 'Approved' as acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. Although listing and labeling are common methods of demonstrating suitability, the ultimate determination of approval rests with the AHJ.

questions.question: A 'Branch Circuit' is the circuit conductors between which two points?
choices: The utility transformer secondary terminals and the service equipment
The service equipment and the first overcurrent protective device downstream
The final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets served
The panelboard bus and the utility metering equipment
questions.answer: The final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets served
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Branch Circuit as the circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlet(s). The 'final' overcurrent device is the last OCPD in the circuit before the outlets — typically a circuit breaker or fuse in a panelboard.

questions.question: How is a 'Feeder' defined in the NEC?
choices: The conductors between the utility service point and the first overcurrent device
All circuit conductors between the service equipment and the final branch-circuit overcurrent device
The conductors between the meter base and the main disconnect
The conductors supplying a motor branch circuit from the motor control center
questions.answer: All circuit conductors between the service equipment and the final branch-circuit overcurrent device
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Feeder as all circuit conductors between the service equipment, the source of a separately derived system, or other supply source and the final branch-circuit overcurrent protective device. Feeders carry power from the service to sub-panels or other distribution equipment.

questions.question: A 'Dwelling Unit' is defined as a unit that provides which of the following?
choices: Sleeping accommodations for not fewer than two persons
Complete and independent living facilities for one or more persons, including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation
A single room used primarily for sleeping and bathing, without a kitchen
A unit in a multi-family building with at least 500 square feet of habitable space
questions.answer: Complete and independent living facilities for one or more persons, including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Dwelling Unit as a single unit providing complete and independent living facilities for one or more persons, including permanent provisions for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation. The key element is the complete living facilities, including cooking — which distinguishes a dwelling unit from a hotel room.

questions.question: Equipment is 'Listed' when it meets which criteria?
choices: Approved in writing by the authority having jurisdiction for a specific installation
Identified in a list published by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (NRTL) that evaluates the equipment for safety
Labeled with a trademark of the manufacturer and meets ANSI product standards
Installed per the manufacturer's instructions and inspected by the AHJ
questions.answer: Identified in a list published by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (NRTL) that evaluates the equipment for safety
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines 'Listed' as equipment, materials, or services included in a list published by an organization that is acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction and concerned with evaluation of products or services. The listing organization (e.g., UL, ETL) periodically inspects production of listed equipment and states that the equipment meets appropriate designated standards or is suitable for a specified purpose.

questions.question: An 'Outlet' is best described as which of the following?
choices: A female receptacle device installed in a box to accept a plug
A point in the wiring system where current is taken to supply utilization equipment
Any junction box where conductors are spliced or connected
A device that controls the flow of current to a load
questions.answer: A point in the wiring system where current is taken to supply utilization equipment
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Outlet as a point in the wiring system at which current is taken to supply utilization equipment. This is a broad definition that includes receptacle outlets, lighting outlets, and appliance outlets — not just receptacles.

questions.question: A 'Raceway' is defined as which type of structure?
choices: A metallic or nonmetallic tube designed to support cables without enclosing them
An enclosed channel of metallic or nonmetallic materials designed expressly for holding wires, cables, or busbars
Any conduit or cable tray used to route conductors between panels
A wireway or gutter used only for exposed surface-mounted wiring
questions.answer: An enclosed channel of metallic or nonmetallic materials designed expressly for holding wires, cables, or busbars
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Raceway as an enclosed channel of metallic or nonmetallic materials designed expressly for holding wires, cables, or busbars, along with their fittings. Raceways include conduits (rigid metal, rigid nonmetallic, flexible), electrical metallic tubing (EMT), wireways, and similar enclosed systems.

questions.question: Equipment is considered to be 'In Sight From' other equipment when which conditions are both met?
choices: The equipment is in the same room and within 25 feet
The equipment is visible and not more than 50 feet (15 m) distant from the other equipment
The equipment is visible and not more than 100 feet (30 m) distant
The equipment is on the same floor level and visible through a window
questions.answer: The equipment is visible and not more than 50 feet (15 m) distant from the other equipment
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines 'In Sight From' (or 'Within Sight From,' 'Within Sight') as visible AND not more than 15 m (50 ft) distant. Both conditions — visibility and distance — must be satisfied. If either condition is not met, the equipment is not 'in sight from' the other equipment.

questions.question: 'Overcurrent' refers to which condition?
choices: Any current flow that causes a visible arc or spark in the electrical system
Current in excess of the rated current of equipment or the ampacity of a conductor, which may result from overload, short circuit, or ground fault
Current that exceeds 125% of the conductor's ampacity for more than three hours
Current that flows in the grounded conductor of a circuit simultaneously with the hot conductor
questions.answer: Current in excess of the rated current of equipment or the ampacity of a conductor, which may result from overload, short circuit, or ground fault
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Overcurrent as any current in excess of the rated current of equipment or the ampacity of a conductor. It may result from overload, short circuit, or ground fault. Overcurrent protection is required by the NEC to protect conductors and equipment from the thermal and mechanical damage caused by excessive current.

questions.question: When equipment is listed or labeled, how must it be installed?
choices: Per the NEC article covering that equipment type, regardless of the manufacturer's instructions
In accordance with any instructions included in the listing or labeling
In any manner acceptable to the AHJ, whether or not it follows the listing instructions
Per the most recent edition of the applicable ANSI product standard
questions.answer: In accordance with any instructions included in the listing or labeling
questions.explanation: NEC 110.3(B) requires that listed or labeled equipment be installed and used in accordance with any instructions included in the listing or labeling. This section effectively makes the manufacturer's listing instructions enforceable NEC requirements — a critical concept tested on licensing exams.

questions.question: The NEC requires that electrical equipment be installed in what manner?
choices: In a listed enclosure rated for the installation environment
In a neat and workmanlike manner
With all conductors labeled and color-coded per Article 200
Per the specifications of a licensed professional engineer
questions.answer: In a neat and workmanlike manner
questions.explanation: NEC 110.12 states that electrical equipment shall be installed in a neat and workmanlike manner. Informational notes reference industry standards such as ANSI/NECA 1 (Standard for Good Workmanship in Electrical Construction) as a guide for determining neat and workmanlike installation.

questions.question: What temperature rating column must be used when selecting the ampacity of conductors connected to equipment rated 100 amperes or less, or for conductors 14 AWG through 1 AWG?
choices: The 75°C column of the applicable ampacity table, regardless of conductor insulation rating
The 90°C column because it yields the highest allowable ampacity
The 60°C column, unless the equipment is marked otherwise
The column matching the conductor's actual insulation temperature rating
questions.answer: The 60°C column, unless the equipment is marked otherwise
questions.explanation: NEC 110.14(C)(1)(a) requires that for equipment rated 100 amperes or less, or for conductors 14 AWG through 1 AWG, the ampacity must be determined using the 60°C column of Table 310.16 (or Table 310.18), unless the equipment is listed and marked for use with conductors at higher temperatures. This prevents overloading equipment terminals with conductor sizes based on higher temperature ratings.

questions.question: Which requirement applies to field-applied hazard markings on electrical equipment?
choices: They must be written in permanent marker and signed by the installer
They must be permanently affixed to the equipment and must not be handwritten
They are required only for equipment operating above 600 volts
They must match the exact wording of the applicable NEC section
questions.answer: They must be permanently affixed to the equipment and must not be handwritten
questions.explanation: NEC 110.21(B) requires that field-applied hazard markings be durably legible, permanently affixed to the equipment, and not handwritten. The marking must also be of adequate size and appropriate color contrast to be clearly visible. Handwritten markings do not meet this requirement because they may fade, smear, or be illegible.

questions.question: What is the minimum dedicated equipment space required above electrical equipment such as a panelboard installed in a building?
choices: The width and depth of the equipment extending from the floor to the ceiling of the room
The width and depth of the equipment extending from the floor to a height of 1.8 m (6 ft) above the equipment, or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower
A zone 1 m (3 ft) wide and 1 m (3 ft) deep in front of the equipment
The full room volume if the room is dedicated to electrical equipment only
questions.answer: The width and depth of the equipment extending from the floor to a height of 1.8 m (6 ft) above the equipment, or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower
questions.explanation: NEC 110.26(E)(1)(a) defines the dedicated equipment space for indoor installations as the footprint (width and depth) of the electrical equipment, extending from the floor to 1.8 m (6 ft) above the top of the equipment, or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. No piping, ducts, leak protection apparatus, or other equipment foreign to the electrical installation is permitted in this zone.

questions.question: How is 'Ground Fault' defined?
choices: An intentional connection between a circuit conductor and the earth for lightning protection

An unintentional, electrically conducting connection between an ungrounded conductor of an electrical circuit and the normally non–current-carrying conductors, metallic enclosures, metallic raceways, metallic equipment, or earth
A condition where both ungrounded conductors of a two-wire circuit contact each other
A low-impedance path intentionally created between the grounding electrode and the equipment enclosure
questions.answer: An unintentional, electrically conducting connection between an ungrounded conductor of an electrical circuit and the normally non–current-carrying conductors, metallic enclosures, metallic raceways, metallic equipment, or earth
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Ground Fault as an unintentional, electrically conducting connection between an ungrounded conductor of an electrical circuit and the normally non–current-carrying conductors, metallic enclosures, metallic raceways, metallic equipment, or earth. Ground faults can result in overcurrent, electric shock, and equipment damage.

questions.question: What is the 'Equipment Grounding Conductor' (EGC)?
choices: The conductor that connects the grounded (neutral) point of the system to a grounding electrode

The conductive path(s) that provide a ground fault current path and connects normally non–current-carrying metal parts of equipment to the system grounded conductor, the grounding electrode conductor, or both
The conductor intentionally connected to earth at the utility transformer secondary
The neutral conductor of a multiwire branch circuit
questions.answer: The conductive path(s) that provide a ground fault current path and connects normally non–current-carrying metal parts of equipment to the system grounded conductor, the grounding electrode conductor, or both
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines the Equipment Grounding Conductor (EGC) as the conductive path(s) installed to provide a ground fault current path and to connect normally non–current-carrying metal parts of equipment to the system grounded conductor, the grounding electrode conductor, or both at the service equipment or source of a separately derived system. The EGC facilitates overcurrent device operation during a ground fault.

questions.question: A 'Grounding Electrode Conductor' (GEC) is defined as the conductor used to connect which components?
choices: The equipment grounding conductor to the grounded service conductor at the main panel
The system grounded conductor or the equipment to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system
The neutral bus of a panelboard to the grounding bus in a subpanel
The grounding electrode to the equipment grounding conductor at each outlet
questions.answer: The system grounded conductor or the equipment to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines the Grounding Electrode Conductor (GEC) as the conductor used to connect the system grounded conductor or the equipment to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system. The GEC provides the essential connection between the electrical system and the earth (grounding electrode), stabilizing the system voltage relative to earth.

questions.question: What is the 'Service Point' as defined by the NEC?
choices: The point of connection between the utility transformer secondary terminals and the service entrance conductors
The point of connection between the facilities of the serving utility and the premises wiring
The location of the utility meter socket on the premises
The main service disconnect where the service conductors terminate
questions.answer: The point of connection between the facilities of the serving utility and the premises wiring
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Service Point as the point of connection between the facilities of the serving utility and the premises wiring. The service point is where utility responsibility ends and the owner's responsibility (and NEC jurisdiction) begins. Conductors on the utility side of the service point are not covered by the NEC.

questions.question: 'Service Equipment' consists of which of the following?
choices: All conductors from the utility transformer to the customer's meter

The necessary equipment, usually consisting of a circuit breaker(s) or switch(es) and fuse(s) and their accessories, connected to the load end of service conductors to constitute the main control and means of cutoff for the supply to a building or structure
Only the utility meter base and associated meter enclosure
The panelboard or load center located closest to the service entrance conductors
questions.answer: The necessary equipment, usually consisting of a circuit breaker(s) or switch(es) and fuse(s) and their accessories, connected to the load end of service conductors to constitute the main control and means of cutoff for the supply to a building or structure
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Service Equipment as the necessary equipment — usually consisting of a circuit breaker(s) or switch(es) and fuse(s) and their accessories — connected to the load end of service conductors to constitute the main control and cutoff means for the building or structure. This is typically referred to as the 'main panel' or 'main disconnect.'

questions.question: When the term is applied to wiring methods (as opposed to equipment), what does 'Accessible' mean?
choices: Can be removed or exposed without damaging the building structure or finish
Can be reached quickly in an emergency without the use of a tool or key
Is within 1.8 m (6 ft) of the floor and in front of the electrical equipment
Is not permanently enclosed and can be inspected without dismantling
questions.answer: Can be removed or exposed without damaging the building structure or finish
questions.explanation: Article 100 gives two distinct definitions of Accessible. When applied to wiring methods, 'Accessible' means capable of being removed or exposed without damaging the building structure or finish, or not permanently closed in by the structure or finish of the building. When applied to equipment, it means admitting close approach — not guarded by locked doors or elevated position. The distinction is critical on licensing exams.

questions.question: A 'Continuous Load' is a load where the maximum current is expected to continue for how long?
choices: 15 minutes or more
30 minutes or more
3 hours or more
8 hours or more
questions.answer: 3 hours or more
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Continuous Load as a load where the maximum current is expected to continue for 3 hours or more. This definition is important because NEC 210.20(A) and 215.3 require that branch circuit and feeder overcurrent devices and conductors be sized at 125% of the continuous load (plus 100% of non-continuous load).

questions.question: The term 'Disconnecting Means' refers to which of the following?
choices: Only fuses and circuit breakers that interrupt fault current
A device or group of devices — or other means — by which conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source of supply
A lockable switch required on all circuits over 150 volts to ground
The main service breaker only, at the point of entry to a building
questions.answer: A device or group of devices — or other means — by which conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source of supply
questions.explanation: Article 100 defines Disconnecting Means as a device, or group of devices, or other means by which the conductors of a circuit can be disconnected from their source of supply. This broad definition includes circuit breakers, switches, plug-and-receptacle combinations, and other devices, not just circuit breakers.

questions.question: Terminals for connecting conductors must be suitable for what?
choices: The conductor's insulation type and voltage rating only
The temperature rating of the conductor insulation
The material of the conductor — aluminum terminals for aluminum conductors, copper terminals for copper conductors, or terminals listed for use with both
The short-circuit current rating of the connected equipment
questions.answer: The material of the conductor — aluminum terminals for aluminum conductors, copper terminals for copper conductors, or terminals listed for use with both
questions.explanation: NEC 110.14(A) requires that terminals shall be suitable for the conductor material. Terminals that are designed only for copper conductors must not be used with aluminum conductors. CO/ALR-rated devices and terminals marked 'AL/CU' are listed for use with both aluminum and copper conductors. Using an incompatible terminal with aluminum can result in overheating and fire.

questions.question: How must splices in conductors be made?
choices: By twisting conductors together and applying electrical tape
With devices identified for the use, or by brazing, welding, or soldering with a fusible metal or alloy
With wire nuts rated for not less than 300 volts in all applications
With listed connectors torqued to the manufacturer's specifications only
questions.answer: With devices identified for the use, or by brazing, welding, or soldering with a fusible metal or alloy
questions.explanation: NEC 110.14(B) requires that conductors be spliced or joined with splicing devices identified for the use, or by brazing, welding, or soldering with a fusible metal or alloy. Soldered splices must be first spliced mechanically then soldered. Splices must be covered with an equivalent insulation. Simply twisting conductors together — even with tape — does not satisfy this requirement.

questions.question: What temperature rating column is used to determine conductor ampacity for equipment rated over 100 amperes, or for conductors larger than 1 AWG?
choices: 60°C column only
75°C column, unless equipment is otherwise marked
90°C column, because larger conductors have higher heat dissipation capacity
The column matching the insulation rating of the conductor, regardless of equipment rating
questions.answer: 75°C column, unless equipment is otherwise marked
questions.explanation: NEC 110.14(C)(1)(b) states that for equipment rated over 100 amperes, or conductors larger than 1 AWG, the ampacity shall be determined using the 75°C column of Table 310.16 or Table 310.18, unless the equipment is listed and marked for use at higher temperatures. This allows larger conductors to take advantage of the 75°C ampacity without overloading the equipment terminals.

questions.question: Which of the following types of electrical equipment must be field-marked to warn qualified persons of the potential electric arc flash hazard?
choices: All electrical equipment rated over 120 volts
Service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, industrial control panels, and motor control centers in other than dwelling units
Only equipment operating at 480 volts or higher
Any equipment with a short-circuit current rating less than the available fault current at the point of installation
questions.answer: Service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, industrial control panels, and motor control centers in other than dwelling units
questions.explanation: NEC 110.16(A) requires that service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures, and motor control centers in other than dwelling units be field-marked to warn qualified persons of the potential electric arc flash hazard. The marking must be located so it is visible before examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance of the equipment.

questions.question: What is the minimum required depth of working space in front of electrical equipment for voltage to ground of 0 to 150 volts (Condition 1)?
choices: 600 mm (2 ft)
900 mm (3 ft)
questions.answer: 900 mm (3 ft)
questions.explanation: NEC 110.26(A)(1) and Table 110.26(A)(1) require a minimum working space depth of 900 mm (3 ft) for equipment operating at 0 to 150 volts to ground under Condition 1 (exposed live parts on one side, no live or grounded parts on the other). Working space depth increases for higher voltages and more hazardous conditions (Conditions 2 and 3).

questions.question: What is the minimum required width of the working space in front of electrical equipment?
choices: 600 mm (24 in.) or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater
750 mm (30 in.) or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater
900 mm (36 in.) or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater
1.0 m (42 in.) regardless of the equipment width
questions.answer: 750 mm (30 in.) or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater
questions.explanation: NEC 110.26(A)(2) requires that the width of the working space in front of electrical equipment be not less than 750 mm (30 in.) or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater. The working space must always be sufficient to permit the equipment to be opened. The working space does not need to be dedicated to the electrical installation.

questions.question: What is required for all electrical equipment rooms and enclosures containing service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards, or motor control centers?
choices: A dedicated HVAC system to maintain equipment within rated operating temperature
Adequate illumination of the working space about electrical equipment
A minimum of two means of egress for rooms larger than 14 m² (150 ft²)
Signage identifying the voltage level of all equipment within the space
questions.answer: Adequate illumination of the working space about electrical equipment
questions.explanation: NEC 110.26(D) requires that the working space about electrical equipment be provided with adequate illumination. The lighting outlets must be arranged so that persons servicing the equipment are not in danger from live parts, and control of the lighting must be accessible without entering the working space in certain conditions. Proper lighting is essential for safe operation and maintenance.
